title: Qi
description: Vital force in traditional Chinese philosophy
wiki_lead:
In the Sinosphere and Chinese philosophy, qi ( CHEE; simplified Chinese: 气; traditional Chinese: 氣; pinyin: qì) is a vital force traditionally believed to be a part of all living entities. Literally meaning 'vapor', 'air', 'gas', or 'breath', the word qi is polysemous, often translated as 'vital energy', 'vital force', 'material energy', or simply 'energy'. Qi is also a concept in traditional Chinese medicine and in Chinese martial arts. The attempt to cultivate and balance qi is called qigong.
Believers in qi describe it as a vital force, with one's good health requiring its flow to be unimpeded. Originally prescientific, today it is a pseudoscientific concept, i.e. not corresponding to the concept of energy as used in the physical sciences.
Chinese gods and immortals, especially anthropomorphic gods, are sometimes thought to have qi and be a reflection of the microcosm of qi in humans, both having qi that can concentrate in certain body parts.

In the Sinosphere and Chinese philosophy, qi ( CHEE; simplified Chinese: 气; traditional Chinese: 氣; pinyin: qì) is a vital force traditionally believed to be a part of all living entities. Literally meaning 'vapor', 'air', 'gas', or 'breath', the word qi is polysemous, often translated as 'vital energy', 'vital force', 'material energy', or simply 'energy'. Qi is also a concept in traditional Chinese medicine and in Chinese martial arts. The attempt to cultivate and balance qi is called qigong.
Believers in qi describe it as a vital force, with one's good health requiring its flow to be unimpeded. Originally prescientific, today it is a pseudoscientific concept, i.e. not corresponding to the concept of energy as used in the physical sciences.

Linguistic aspects

The cultural keyword qì is analyzable in terms of Chinese and Sino-Xenic pronunciations. It is represented by the logographs 氣, 气, and 気 with various meanings ranging from "vapor" to "anger", and is the source of the English loanword qi or ch'i.


Pronunciation and etymology
The logograph 氣 is read with two Chinese pronunciations: the usual qì 氣 "air; vital energy" and the rare archaic xì 氣 "to present food" (later disambiguated with 餼). Hackett Publishing Company, Philip J. Ivanhoe, and Bryan W. Van Norden theorize that the word qi possibly came from a term that referred to "the mist that arose from heated sacrificial offerings".
Pronunciations of 氣 in modern varieties of Chinese with standardized IPA equivalents include: Standard Chinese qì /t͡ɕʰi˥˩/, Wu Chinese qi /t͡ɕʰi˧˦/, Southern Min khì /kʰi˨˩/, Eastern Min ké /kʰɛi˨˩˧/, Standard Cantonese hei3 /hei̯˧/, and Hakka Chinese hi /hi˥/.
Pronunciations of 氣 in Sino-Xenic borrowings include: Japanese ki, Korean gi, and Vietnamese khí.
Reconstructions of the Middle Chinese pronunciation of 氣 standardized to IPA transcription include: /kʰe̯iH/ (Bernard Karlgren), /kʰĭəiH/ (Wang Li), /kʰiəiH/ (Li Rong), /kʰɨjH/ (Edwin Pulleyblank), and /kʰɨiH/ (Zhengzhang Shangfang).
Axel Schuessler's reconstruction of the Later Han Chinese pronunciation of 氣 is /kɨs/.
Reconstructions of the Old Chinese pronunciation of 氣 standardized to IPA transcription include: */kʰɯds/ (Zhengzhang Shangfang), */C.qʰəp-s/ (William H. Baxter and Laurent Sagart), and */kə(t)s/ (Axel Schuessler).
The etymology of qì interconnects with Kharia kʰis "anger", Sora kissa "move with great effort", Khmer kʰɛs "strive after; endeavor", and Gyalrongic kʰɐs "anger".


Characters
In the East Asian languages, qì has three logographs:

氣 is the traditional Chinese character, Korean hanja, and Japanese kyūjitai ("old character form") kanji
気 is the Japanese shinjitai ("new character form") kanji
气 is the simplified Chinese character.
In addition, qì 炁 is an uncommon character especially used in writing Daoist talismans. Historically, the word qì was generally written as 气 until the Han dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE), when it was replaced by the 氣 graph clarified with mǐ 米 "rice" indicating "steam (rising from rice as it cooks.)" and depicting the Traditional Chinese view of the transformative, changeable nature of existence and the universe.
This primary logograph 气, the earliest written character for qì, consisted of three wavy horizontal lines seen in Shang dynasty (c. 1600–1046 BCE) oracle bone script, Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BCE) bronzeware script and large seal script, and Qin dynasty (221–206 BCE) small seal script. These oracle, bronze, and seal scripts logographs 气 were used in ancient times as a phonetic loan character to write qǐ 乞 "plead for; beg; ask" which did not have an early character.

grok_lead: Qi (æ°£), often translated as "vital energy" or "life force," is a foundational concept in ancient Chinese philosophy and traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), representing the dynamic energy that permeates and constitutes all matter, phenomena, and living beings in the universe. This all-encompassing force is neither purely material nor immaterial but encompasses both, driving processes of growth, change, and harmony while manifesting in dual forms of constructive (healing) and destructive (pathogenic) influences. Originating in pre-modern Chinese thought, Qi is depicted in classical texts as arising from states of calm, emptiness, and non-desiring, as articulated in the Huangdi Neijing (Yellow Emperor's Inner Canon), a cornerstone medical text compiled around the 2nd century BCE. In Chinese philosophy, Qi serves as the basic substance underlying cosmology and ontology, organizing matter and events in a microcosm-macrocosm analogy where human vitality mirrors cosmic patterns. Early references appear in Warring States period works like the Zhuangzi (circa 4thâ3rd century BCE), which links Qi to human formation from heavenly and earthly energies, while Han dynasty syntheses integrated it with yin-yang duality and the wuxing (five phases) to explain natural and bodily dynamics. Philosophers such as Mencius (372â289 BCE) further characterized Qi as a moral and ethical energy tied to human excellence and self-cultivation, emphasizing its role in nurturing life ( yang sheng) for longevity and harmony. Within TCM, Qi is the vital force regulating physiological functions, circulating through a network of meridians and supporting organ systems ( zang-fu), with imbalancesâsuch as stagnation, deficiency, or excessâleading to illness. Therapeutics like acupuncture stimulate specific acupoints to restore Qi flow, addressing conditions from chronic pain to digestive disorders, while herbal medicine employs substances (e.g., ginseng to tonify Qi) tailored to individual patterns based on ancient principles from the Huangdi Neijing. Practices such as Qigong and Tai Chi cultivate and manipulate Qi for health maintenance, reflecting its integration into broader Daoist traditions of bodily and spiritual refinement.
